title: SaaS Procurement Guide: A Practical Checklist From Request to Renewal
description: A repeatable SaaS purchasing process covering requirements, security review, vendor evidence, contract terms, total cost, rollout ownership, and renewal decisions.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Create a Purchase Request With a Clear Owner
sections.body: Start every request with the business problem, the affected workflow, the number and roles of users, the systems involved, and the outcome expected. Record the current workaround and its cost in time, errors, risk, or missed opportunities. Name a business owner and a technical or administrative owner. This avoids buying a tool because a team saw a demo or because another department uses it. If an existing tool can meet the requirement with a small configuration change, compare that option before introducing another vendor.

sections.title: Define Requirements and Alternatives
sections.body: Separate mandatory requirements from preferences. Mandatory requirements may include data protection, access control, integrations, accessibility, data export, regional needs, or an operational deadline. Preferences might include a particular interface or extra automation. Compare at least one credible alternative, including extending the current stack or doing nothing. Use a scorecard with evidence for each criterion and mark unknowns explicitly. Require vendors to show the workflow in the product or document the capability in writing; do not treat a roadmap promise as a delivered feature.

sections.title: Complete Security, Privacy, and Legal Checks
sections.body: Review the data the service will process, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, and how it can be exported or deleted. Check authentication, role permissions, audit logs, incident notification, subprocessors, and the vendor's current security documentation. Legal or compliance teams should review terms that matter to the organization's obligations, including data processing and confidentiality. Do not collect sensitive data in a trial until the required safeguards are approved. Record any exception, its owner, and the date by which it must be resolved.

sections.title: Calculate Total Cost, Not Just Subscription Price
sections.body: Estimate cost over a common period such as 12 or 36 months. Include seats, minimum commitments, usage charges, add-ons, implementation, migration, training, integration work, administration, support, and renewal changes. Ask how discounts change at renewal and whether removing users affects the contract. Model a conservative usage scenario and a growth scenario. For a CRM or sales platform, include the effort needed to clean contacts, map pipeline stages, and maintain integrations; those tasks can be material even when the subscription price is straightforward.

sections.title: Pilot the Contracted Workflow
sections.body: Before signing a long commitment, test the most important workflow with realistic but approved data. Include normal use, an exception, permissions, export, and the integration that would be hardest to replace. Agree on pass/fail criteria in advance and involve the people who will administer the service. Keep a record of claims that were demonstrated, claims confirmed in documentation, and items that remain open. If a vendor offers a proof of concept, clarify who owns the configuration and whether it can be reused after purchase.

sections.title: Negotiate Terms and Plan the Exit
sections.body: Confirm contract duration, renewal notice period, price changes, user minimums, support commitments, service availability terms where relevant, data ownership, export format, deletion process, and any fees for leaving. Assign ownership of administrator accounts and integration credentials to the organization rather than a single employee. Identify how data will be retrieved and how access will be revoked if the vendor relationship ends. An exit plan is not a prediction that the product will fail; it reduces lock-in and makes the purchase easier to govern.

sections.title: Review Usage Before Renewal
sections.body: Set a review date before the renewal notice deadline. Compare actual usage, user feedback, support requests, outcomes against the baseline, and total cost with the original business case. Check for duplicate tools and unused seats, but do not remove licenses without confirming business needs. Decide whether to renew, renegotiate, reduce scope, or migrate. Keep the decision and its evidence in a central record so future procurement starts with what the organization learned rather than repeating the same discovery process.
